{{Short description|Mathematical constant about polygons}}
[[File:Bouwkamp1.svg|thumb|A sequence of inscribed circles and [[regular polygons]] with increasing numbers of sides, which converge towards a circle at the [[Limit of a function|limit]].]]

In [[plane geometry]], the '''Kepler–Bouwkamp constant''' (or '''polygon inscribing constant''') is obtained as a [[limit of a sequence|limit]] of the following [[sequence]]. Take a [[circle]] of radius&nbsp;1. [[Inscribed figure|Inscribe]] a [[Equilateral triangle|regular triangle]] in this circle. Inscribe a circle in this triangle. Inscribe a [[Square (geometry)|square]] in it. Inscribe a circle, [[Pentagon|regular pentagon]], circle, [[Hexagon|regular hexagon]] and so forth. 
The [[radius]] of the limiting circle is called the Kepler–Bouwkamp constant.<ref>{{cite book|first1=S. R. |last1=Finch|author1-link=Steven R. Finch |title=Mathematical Constants |url=https://archive.org/details/mathematicalcons0000finc |url-access=registration |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2003|isbn=9780521818056 |mr=2003519}}</ref> It is named after [[Johannes Kepler]] and {{interlanguage link|Christoffel Jacob Bouwkamp|de}}, and is the inverse of the [[polygon circumscribing constant]].

==Numerical value==
{{unsolved|mathematics|Is the Kepler–Bouwkamp constant irrational?}}
The decimal expansion of the Kepler–Bouwkamp constant is {{OEIS|A085365}}
<math display=block> \prod_{k=3}^\infty \cos \frac\pi k = 0.1149420448\dots. </math>
The natural logarithm of the Kepler-Bouwkamp constant is given by 
<math display=block>-2\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac{2^{2k}-1}{2k}\zeta(2k)\left(\zeta(2k)-1-\frac{1}{2^{2k}}\right)</math>  

where <math>\zeta(s) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^s}</math> is the [[Riemann zeta function]].

If the product is taken over the [[odd prime]]s, the constant
<math display=block>\prod_{{k\,=\,3,\,5,\,7,\atop 11,\,13,\,17,\,\ldots}} \!\!\!\cos \frac\pi k = 
0.312832\ldots</math>
is obtained {{OEIS|A131671}}.
